newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan hails child labour agreement.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan hails child labour agreement.

text.p: Pakistani authorities on Saturday hailed a plan end the use of child labour in the soccer ball industry in Pakistan.
A spokesman for the Ministry of Labour and Manpower told Reuters that the government wanted an end to child labour in Pakistan.
"We are encouraging all such steps that lead towards elimination of child labour and extend our full cooperation," he said.
The spokesman said Pakistan, faced with international criticism and threats of trade sanctions, had started taking stern action against factories employing child labour.
Officials say Pakistans provincial labour departments began a crackdown on child labour abuse and conducted more than 7,000 raids on various businesses between January 1995 and March 1996.
Authorities prosecuted 2,538 employers, of whom 395 were convicted and fined under child labour laws though they were let off after paying fines.

The International Labour Organisation (ILO), child welfare advocates and sporting goods manufacturers announced a plan on Friday in Atlanta to try to end the use of child labour in making soccer balls in Pakistan.
At least 7,000 children work full time in Pakistan stitching two-thirds of the worlds soccer balls.
The ILO has signed an agreement with makers such as Adidas, Nike and Reebok and industrialists in Pakistan to remove child labourers from the industry.

The city of Sialkot, the centre of Pakistans sports goods industry, produces two-thirds of the worlds hand-stitched soccer balls for an export market worth $1 billion a year in retail sales, the ILO said.
Under the deal, the ILO will help soccer ball manufacturers to remove child labourers from their work with the help of financing from the U.S. government and the Soccer Industry Council of America.

In Pakistan, the ILO will cooperate with Sialkots Chamber of Commerce and Industry to monitor the industry, increase awareness of child labour among producers and assist children removed from the workplace, its statement said.
Pakistans first child labour survey in collaboration with the ILO last October showed that 3.6 million children aged between five and 14 years were working full time in the country.
